paras: The beating of an unnamed Black man in Webster Parish, Louisiana, took place in August 1881, when neighbors gave a man accused of attempting to outrage a Mrs. Crow 'a sound thrashing' and ordered him to leave the country. No death was reported, and the episode is known from a single paragraph in the Richland Beacon's column of Louisiana state news, whose editor wrote that the neighbors 'ought to have broken his neck.'

According to the Richland Beacon, a man it called a 'negro brute' attempted to outrage Mrs. Crow in Webster Parish during the week before its 27 August issue. Her husband was reported to have arrived in time to rescue her and to 'arrest the scoundrel' himself. Neighbors were then called in, and they beat the man and ordered him to leave the country. The paragraph names no town, gives no names other than Mrs. Crow's, and does not state the races of the Crows or the neighbors.
No report of the man being handed to officers, of any arrest of the neighbors, or of his fate after he was ordered away appears in the coverage.

The Richland Beacon ran the item on 27 August 1881 in its 'Among our State Exchanges' column, between notes on a Minden newspaper's anniversary and a hailstorm near Minden, without naming the paper it drew from. It stated the accusation as fact, called the accused 'the scoundrel', and closed with the comment 'They ought to have broken his neck.' No other report of the episode, and no Black-press account, was found.
